newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Beehive-Rival views of NZ economy.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Beehive-Rival views of NZ economy.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Dec 3 - The authors of the December economic and fiscal update and ACT's "The deepening crisis in the countryside" -- both issued in Wellington on Monday -- could have been writing about different countries.

While caretaker Finance Minister Bill Birch was reporting cheerfully that the incoming government would inherit an economy on a high sustainable growth path, and a strengthening fiscal position, ACT's rural spokesman Owen Jennings had the worry beads out: government spending was, he claimed, killing rural industry.

Birch concedes that farmers are finding it difficult, with the rise in the exchange rate putting further pressure on the competitiveness of exporters -- but he says they are better placed to respond effectively to these increased pressures than they were in the late 1980s when confronted with similar rises in the exchange rate.

The government, he adds, is implementing a $15.5 billion programme in initiatives over the three years to 1997/98. These include increased priority spending, debt repayment and tax reductions, and are designed to provide the maximum social return to New Zealanders within the limits of prudence.

But ACT, by implication, ridicules the Birch scenario. It contends the dollar is over-valued, and the export industries are in desperate straits. The only way to bring interest rates down (and thereby the level of the dollar) is to bring public spending back under control.

Government spending has gone up more than 15 percent in the last three years -- an extra four billion dollars a year is being pumped into the economy. That "excessive" spending is driving up inflation and has led New Zealand to carry the burden of the highest real interest rates in the world.
ACT has called on the government to commit to an immediate programme of disciplined expenditure, with no government spending increases for the next two years.
"The stark reality is that by this time next year, 8,000 properties could be in severe trouble, with maybe 30,000 people moving off the land," says ACT.

Treasury's view of the rural economy, as presented in the DEFU, contrasts sharply with that of ACT. It says that, on average, farm incomes are rising slowly. While returns from sheep and beef farming are continuing to decline, dairy incomes have been lifted by a combination of high international prices
It accepts that trading conditions for exporters will remain difficult but sees a more positive outlook. Non-commodity export growth is expected to rebound in 1997/98.

Labour, like ACT, thinks that the effects of the high-flying Kiwi dollar are coming home to roost. Finance spokesman Michael Cullen says the DEFU, with its faith in consumption-led growth and acknowledgment that the tradeables sector will continue to lag, suggests that neither Treasury nor the caretaker National government have grasped the nature, or the urgency of, or the action needed to deal with, the issues facing the NZ economy.

Cullen resists the ACT conclusion: the answer is not to punish the poor or to bankrupt health and education services. Instead it should attack directly the cause of the present problems: the high exchange rate.
That would be his first priority, he says, as minister of finance in a Labour-led government.

NZ First's Winston Peters, judging by his public statements, might agree with Cullen on the high exchange rate. But Peters seems to be taking a different tack than Cullen over public sending: his party fears a fiscal blow-out under Labour.
NZ First has consistently taken a gloomier view of the economy than has Treasury or Labour -- and the revisions downwards, admittedly slight, in Treasury's forecasts may reinforce its queasiness.

If, as Winston Peters told a Tauranga audience on Sunday, "NZ First is not in the business of hocking off its principles to the highest bidder" the question is: how high does fiscal rectitude stand on that list of principles?
Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters
